title: Carving the Story: Women and Sculpture in East Africa
standfirst: From a 2021 online panel on sculpture to a twelve-day women-only workshop in Tuala, NCAI's record of Chelenge Van Rampelberg, Theresa Musoke and their contemporaries shows how women learned and taught three-dimensional work.
bodyMarkdown:
In September 2021, before its Nairobi galleries had opened, the Nairobi Contemporary Art Institute hosted an online conversation about sculpture. On 7 September, Wangechi Mutu, Magdalene Odundo DBE and Chelenge Van Rampelberg joined moderator Mukami Kuria for a panel that followed the Ledge Sculpture intervention at the Royal Academy of Arts in London. NCAI's announcement promised a one-and-a-half-hour conversation and Q&A in which the three artists would discuss their approach to sculpture. The recording remains on the institute's website.

The panel is a useful place to begin, because it did two things at once. It treated sculpture as a field with its own questions, separate from painting, which has long dominated the story told about East African art. And it put a Kenyan sculptor, working in wood on the edge of Nairobi, in the same conversation as two artists with international careers. This essay follows that thread through the work of Chelenge Van Rampelberg and a few of her contemporaries, using what NCAI's exhibitions, collection and publications can document.

## A practice learned by watching

Chelenge Van Rampelberg was born in 1961 in Kericho, in Kenya's Rift Valley. She has no academic training in art. In the artist portrait film NCAI published in 2024, she recalls following the men of her village as they built huts with nails, hammers, saws and machetes. Those are the tools she later used to make sculpture. Her work, the film suggests, stays tied to memories of childhood in the village, and to a nostalgia she describes as a lodestar for how she tries to live.

Her formal route into art began in 1984, at workshops run by Gallery Watatu with the Ngecha Artists Association. She later took courses in etching and woodcut printing at the Alliance Francaise in Nairobi, and her first exhibition followed in 1985. She began as a painter. According to the biography compiled for NCAI, she started to carve after an avocado tree fell outside her house. From there she worked in ebony, jacaranda and other woods; the NCAI film also lists doum palm and sikotoi. The type of wood, with its grain, colour and texture, anchors her vision, the film says.

Her method is closer to listening than to imposing a design. In the film she says: "once I have the wood with me, I pick the story, and I use the wood to bring out that story as the writer would write the book." The artist and writer Zihan Kassam, quoted in the same film notes, puts it from the other side: Van Rampelberg "grants her wood permission to say what it has to", considering its natural curvature and the flow of the grain as she carves tall, amorphous figures.

## Subjects: women, beauty, belonging

The figures she carves are semi-abstract, and they centre on women and their place in society, on black beauty and on gender inequality, alongside religious subjects. Her first sculpture, My Mum and I, is held by NCAI. The institute's collection holds more than 140 of her works, including sculptures, woodcut prints and inked woodcut plates, a substantial holding for a single artist. She has been described in the press as Kenya's first female sculptor. NCAI's own film is more careful, calling her one of Kenya's first female sculptors.

Her work has appeared in four NCAI presentations: Mwili, Akili na Roho (2022), The Long Way Home (2023), 60 Years: the NCAI Collection (2024) and, in 2026, Michael Armitage, Maria Lassnig, Chelenge Van Rampelberg, organised with Kunsthaus Bregenz. ART AFRICA's account of the last describes her woodcuts and wooden sculptures, among them male heads with pursed mouths and upright female figures that convey intimacy and relational sensitivity, with softened contours and restrained gestures evoking connections among people, nature and the living world. The exhibition text says Michael Armitage regards her as a mentor, teacher and friend.

## Teaching the next group

If one measure of an art form's health is who learns it, NCAI offers a small piece of evidence. In early 2024 the institute announced an open call for a women-only sculpting and etching workshop led by Van Rampelberg. Participants would stay at her studio in Tuala for twelve days, with accommodation, food, drink and materials provided, and the call encouraged early-career artists and applicants from outside Nairobi. NCAI's listing dates the workshop to 26 February 2024; the application deadline was 2 February.

The terms of the call are modest and specific. It describes a safe, supportive and creative environment, and a chance to connect with like-minded artists, and it requires participants to be on site for the full period. It treats sculpture as something learned by working alongside someone who knows the material, in the way Van Rampelberg learned it from a workshop and from watching builders.

## Painters and printmakers in the same story

Sculpture is only one of the media in which women artists of her generation worked in the region, and the NCAI Collection shows the others. Theresa Musoke is a Ugandan painter and printmaker, among the first women to earn a fine art degree at Makerere University. In 1965 she became the first woman artist given a solo exhibition at the Uganda Museum in Kampala. She lived in Nairobi from 1974 to 1996 and taught at Kenyatta University and the International School of Kenya. Her semi-abstract work, which uses painting, printmaking, batik and barkcloth, addresses African identity, domestic roles, motherhood and family planning as well as East African wildlife. NCAI holds seven of her works, including Cat Ghosts (1963), and showed her in Mwili, Akili na Roho and 60 Years.

Tabitha wa Thuku, born in 1963, began as a self-taught painter and was one of few women artists of her generation. Her Cracked Bag IV (2024), in the NCAI Collection, is an assemblage of wood, steel and found objects. It sits in the collection alongside Van Rampelberg's carved wood, though the two works come from different practices. In 2022 her work was shown alongside that of Musoke and Yony Waite at Circle Art Gallery in Nairobi, in a retrospective of three artists.

## What the record shows, and what it does not

NCAI is a young institution, established in 2020, and its holdings reflect what it has been able to collect and exhibit so far. They are not a survey of every woman sculptor who has worked in East Africa, and this essay does not claim to be one. What they do show is a set of overlapping lines: apprenticeship in workshops and galleries rather than art schools, wood as a primary material, women as a recurring subject, and a few artists who teach others.

The 2021 panel anticipated that pattern. Three artists spoke about sculpture from different positions, to an audience that could join from anywhere. The conversation was recorded, and the recording is part of the archive that NCAI is building. For anyone studying women's work in three dimensions in East Africa, that is where the record starts, and where more work remains to be done.

title: Sane: Self-Taught Painters in Kenya
standfirst: NCAI opened in 2022 with a survey of Sane Wadu, who renamed himself against his critics. His career shows how self-taught Kenyan painters built their own schools, from Gallery Watatu to the Ngecha Artists Association.
bodyMarkdown:
When the Nairobi Contemporary Art Institute opened its doors in January 2022, its first exhibition was a survey of a painter who had spent four decades outside the academy. I Hope So: Sane Wadu brought together drawings, paintings and prints by an artist who was born in Nyathuna in 1954, taught himself to paint, and took a new name to answer his critics. Writing in frieze, Eric Otieno Sumba called it the first survey of the autodidact's long painting career. The choice of opening show said something about the institute's priorities, and it is worth reading closely.

## A name taken back

Wadu's early biography reads as a series of departures. He worked first as an educator, then as a court clerk, then moved into cultural production as a writer, playwright and theatre actor. NCAI's exhibition text quotes him as saying that he "came to realise these things will not give a way to express [himself] the way [he] wanted to." Painting, which he took up in the early 1980s, was the form that did.

Leaving steady employment for an artist's life cost him socially. His peers labelled him "insane". His response, as the exhibition text puts it, was to rename himself "Sane", a subversive act in defiance of the madness they had ascribed to him. Sumba reads the name the same way, as a counter to the prevailing idea that artists like him were insane.

Sources differ slightly on dates. NCAI gives 1984 as the year he began painting, while frieze says 1983. Red Hill Art Gallery says that when he submitted his first paintings to Gallery Watatu in Nairobi in 1984, the gallery's curator, the late Ruth Schaffner, saw the talent behind rough and impetuous brushwork. It adds that his first experiments involved household paint on plastic sheets and on his own clothes.

## Working without the credentials

Being self-taught carried a commercial cost. NCAI's artist portrait film says that in the 1980s Wadu had to navigate the pedagogical and formal expectations of commercial gallerists, and realised that formally trained artists enjoyed greater success. Gallerists questioned his viability. The turning point, the film says, was his meeting with Ruth Schaffner of Gallery Watatu. Sumba adds that his practice was at first judged too challenging for Kenya's conservative art audiences, and that Schaffner supported him from the start. In the 1980s and 1990s he was one of the artists Watatu promoted.

The same pattern appears in other lives in the NCAI Collection. Chelenge Van Rampelberg, who has no academic training in art, began painting and sculpting in 1984 at Gallery Watatu workshops run with the Ngecha Artists Association. The Ugandan painter Jak Katarikawe, largely self-taught and associated with Paa Ya Paa Arts Centre and Gallery Watatu in Nairobi, developed a narrative, dreamlike figurative style drawn from village life, love and family. Tabitha wa Thuku began as a self-taught artist and later studied at the Buruburu Institute of Fine Arts. These artists have different styles and different routes, but the institutions that sustained them overlap. Gallery Watatu, Paa Ya Paa and the Ngecha community gave them what a conventional art school would otherwise have provided: a place to work, a market and a circle of peers.

## Ngecha as a school

Wadu co-founded the Ngecha Artists Association, with his contemporaries Eunice Wadu, Wanyu Brush and Chain Muhindi, according to NCAI. The institute credits the association with providing critical support and training to generations of Nairobi-based artists. Frieze describes it as a collective of about forty members that built a thriving art community in the village of that name, just outside Nairobi, offering support, training and opportunities. The sources do not agree on when it was founded. Frieze dates it to 1995, while Red Hill Art Gallery places it at the beginning of the 1990s.

In the portrait film, Wadu begins to discuss an egalitarian philosophy and a respect for the subjectivity of the artist, which NCAI describes as underpinning the ethos of the Ngecha community. The point is a practical one. A movement of self-taught artists cannot rely on a curriculum, so it depends on the willingness of its members to teach one another.

## What the paintings do

I Hope So drew on decades of observations, in NCAI's words, about religion, spirituality, gender and politics in Kenyan society. Frieze's review gives some concrete examples. The show opened with Bless This Our Daily Bread (1984), a painting of a bearded figure in a white robe standing over five loaves of bread and two fish. Black Moses (1993) shows a large Black figure surrounded by people in prostration, a godhead who resembles the former president Daniel arap Moi, in a work that the reviewer reads as a criticism of Kenyan leadership's use of Christian ideology. The canvases Night Shift (2000) and Life Conspiracy (2019) show his later use of abstraction and dense colour. Of the works, frieze counted 37 from the 1980s and 1990s and five produced after 2000.

Subversion also operates at the level of technique. NCAI's text says Wadu renounced the academic aspects of painting and conventional expectations of coherence. He deliberately includes text rendered backwards, makes double-sided works, and at times signs works incorrectly, which it describes as small acts that keep questioning the status quo. A trained painter learns to avoid these things; a self-taught one can treat them as a repertoire.

The exhibition text frames Wadu as a traveller, an msafiri, on a journey, and calls the paintings critical but made in consideration of an imminent future in which there is optimism for something better. Sumba notes the same tenacious optimism in the title, which he sets against a career that has not been smooth. He also reads it as pointing to a change in the local art scene that made a survey of this kind possible.

## In conversation

On 19 February 2022, in the retrospective's run, Wadu spoke with Yony Waite in a conversation moderated by Gakunju Kaigwa at NCAI. The event listing noted that the three artists represented approximately a century of art-making between them, and that the exchange would look at Wadu's journey in a historical Kenyan context, and at the changing arts and culture landscape, his influences and those of his contemporaries.

Wadu's work returned in Mwili, Akili na Roho: Ten Figurative Painters from East Africa (October 2022), where he appeared with painters including Katarikawe, Peter Mulindwa and Theresa Musoke, and in 60 Years: the NCAI Collection (2024). That recurrence matters. A self-taught artist who once had trouble getting shows now appears across the institute's programme as one of its reference points.

## A different map

The story of self-taught painters in Kenya is often told in terms of what they lacked. The record NCAI holds suggests another account, in which they built their own educational structures, from Watatu's workshops to the Ngecha association, and made work that other artists learned from. Wadu's career, as NCAI presents it, is the clearest case. He gave himself a name, joined with others to teach, and kept painting. The title of his survey, I Hope So, is a statement that still has to be earned, and the paintings show how.

title: Why an Archive: Collecting and Preserving East African Art
standfirst: A fire at Paa Ya Paa, a collection that spans six decades and a library open for reference: NCAI's own record shows why a young institution builds an archive alongside its exhibitions.
bodyMarkdown:
The Nairobi Contemporary Art Institute describes itself, on its website, as a non-profit visual art space dedicated to the growth and preservation of contemporary art in East Africa. The word "preservation" sits next to "growth" on purpose. NCAI was established in 2020, and from the start its programme has included, alongside exhibitions and public talks, the development of an East African art archive. This essay asks why an art institution should invest in collecting and keeping, and what the evidence from NCAI's own work suggests.

## What gets lost

NCAI's artist portrait of Elimo Njau, the Tanzanian-born painter and founder of the Paa Ya Paa Centre in Nairobi, contains a sentence that explains the problem plainly. In 1998, the film says, a fire ravaged Njau's home and much of the gallery, destroying his works and those of other artists, and "with the fire disappeared a part of Kenyan history". Paa Ya Paa had been, in the film's account, a mainstay for artists and intellectuals including Okot p'Bitek, Taban Lo Liyong and Ngugi wa Thiong'o from its founding. Other sources date the fire to 1997, but both accounts agree on what it destroyed: objects, and with them a record of who gathered where.

That is a loss at the scale of one building. The wider condition is quieter. Much of the history of art in East Africa was made in private studios, community workshops and short-lived galleries, and was recorded, if at all, in newspaper cuttings, exhibition invitations and personal photographs. Such material is fragile and tends to remain in the hands of whoever happened to keep it.

## A collection of six decades

NCAI's permanent collection is its most visible answer. The exhibition 60 Years: the NCAI Collection, shown from August 2024, presents works spanning six decades. The institute's text calls the permanent collection a cornerstone of its mission to promote, preserve and make accessible the history and practice of artmaking in East Africa. It includes works by artists from Kenya, Uganda, Ethiopia, Sudan, the Democratic Republic of Congo and South Africa, with pieces dating back to the 1960s.

The show did not follow a strict chronology. It brought works into dialogue through formal and thematic connections, including artists' engagement with the natural world and figuration as a vehicle for social commentary. It included painting, drawing, printmaking and sculpture, and some thirty artists, among them Josephine Alacu, Rashid Diab, David Koloane, Jak Katarikawe, Peterson Kamwathi, Theresa Musoke and Afewerk Tekle. A collection arranged this way works as an argument about relationships across borders and generations, and not as a catalogue.

Depth matters as much as range. The NCAI Collection holds more than 140 works by Chelenge Van Rampelberg, including sculptures, woodcut prints and the inked woodcut plates from which prints are pulled. It holds fourteen oil paintings by Peter Mulindwa, all on board, including Uganda Martyrs (1968), and seven works by Theresa Musoke, among them Cat Ghosts (1963). It also holds single works that carry weight: Mwenze Kibwanga's Hunting and Harvesting (1968), by a Congolese painter of the Atelier du Hangar. A holding of this kind lets a researcher follow one artist's development, compare plates with prints, and see how a studio worked.

The collection depends on support. NCAI credits White Cube and David Zwirner Gallery, with additional support from Gerd Schwandner, Mercedes Villardell and Dale Matthias, and thanks Villardell for significant contributions to the permanent collection. A collection is the product of sustained patronage, and the institute acknowledges as much.

## Books, papers and the written record

The website describes a second strand: a Library and Archive. With support and book donations from art institutions and galleries in Kenya and abroad, NCAI is building an art library. It is also developing an archive of exhibitions, events and writings that tell the story of the artists and the art of East Africa. The library's catalogue is available online, and the institute states that it is for reference and research only: books may not be borrowed.

The library is also used. In December 2024 NCAI began a series of reading groups led by Ato Malinda, "Diving into the library". The first session paired excerpts from bell hooks's Salvation: Black People and Love with Lynette Yiadom-Boakye: Under-Song for a Cipher, with all the books available at the NCAI Library. Sessions were free, in person, and required registration.

The institute's own output is archival too. Its artist portrait films record artists speaking about their practice, and its press page lists coverage of its exhibitions in ArtAfrica, Daily Monitor, Mount Kenya Times, Art Report Africa and The East African. Together they form a layer of documentation around the works themselves.

## Archives as a method

For some artists NCAI has shown, the archive is a subject as well as a resource. Canon Griffin Rumanzi, who was born in Uganda in 1991, uses digital collage and archival intervention to explore, in NCAI's words, the fragmented and often contradictory nature of Uganda's past. His 2025 solo exhibition, Looking into the Mad Eye of History Without Blinking, combined colonial documents, state symbols and family portraits. He co-founded History in Progress Uganda (HIPUganda) with the artist and educator Andrea Stultiens in 2011. It is a public archive that collects, digitises and republishes photographs from or about Uganda's past, to make the country's visual history accessible and contestable.

In July 2022 the TURN 2 curator-in-residence Nathalie Anguezomo Mba Bikoro led a performing archives workshop at NCAI, "Rasha Will Dismantle the Master's House: Revolt in the Archives". It used materials from the Mohammed Amin Foundation and the Nairobi National Museum to examine relations between the body, recovery and archival research as tools for empowerment, particularly around Black women's narratives in Kenya's history. The workshop was open to artists, curators, researchers, writers and makers.

Both examples make the same point from different directions. An archive is a set of choices about what is kept, how it is described and who may use it. Opening those choices to public inspection, as HIPUganda does, and asking participants to work physically with archival material, as the workshop did, are ways of treating the archive as unfinished.

## Why now

There are three practical reasons. The first is risk: material that is not collected can burn, decay or disperse, as the Paa Ya Paa fire showed. The second is reference. A younger artist, curator or student writing about East African art will need images, catalogues and primary documents in the region, in Nairobi, in a place that is open to them. NCAI's library is limited, reference-only, and still being built, and its mission statement says as much. The third is the shape of the field itself. By collecting across six decades and several countries, NCAI makes it possible to see East African art as a connected conversation, in which a 1968 painting from Katanga, a 1960s oil from Uganda and a 2024 assemblage by a Nairobi artist can hang in the same room.

None of this is finished, and the institute does not claim otherwise: its library is under construction and its archive is being developed. But the argument for starting is clear from the evidence above. What is not recorded can be lost in one night, and what is collected and shared can still be used to make sense of the past.

title: Michael Armitage and Chelenge Van Rampelberg in Conversation
standfirst: On 21 February 2026, two days after a Kunsthaus Bregenz exhibition opened in Nairobi, the artists spoke at NCAI in a talk moderated by Don Handa.
bodyMarkdown:
At the Nairobi Contemporary Art Institute on Saturday 21 February 2026, from 14:00 to 16:00, Michael Armitage and Chelenge Van Rampelberg took part in an artist talk, moderated by Don Handa. It came two days after the opening of Michael Armitage, Maria Lassnig, Chelenge Van Rampelberg, which ran from 19 February to 5 April 2026. NCAI's listing for the talk carries no description beyond the title, so this report does not describe what was said in the room. It sets out who took part, what the conversation was attached to, and why the pairing of these two artists carries weight.

## The participants

Michael Armitage, born in Nairobi in 1984, is a painter who lives and works between London and Nairobi. He is the founder of NCAI, a non-profit platform for contemporary art in East Africa. Chelenge Van Rampelberg, born in Kericho in 1961, is a Kenyan sculptor and printmaker who works mainly in wood from a studio near Nairobi. Don Handa moderated.

The exhibition text describes their relationship directly. Armitage has a long-standing relationship with Van Rampelberg, "one of Kenya's most accomplished artists", and, to him, a mentor, teacher and friend. An artist talk in which the two sit together therefore picks up a thread that runs through the exhibition itself.

## The exhibition behind the talk

The show was presented by NCAI in collaboration with Kunsthaus Bregenz (KUB), where it was first shown in 2025. Nairobi was its second iteration. It brought drawings and lithographs by Armitage together with drawings by the Austrian painter Maria Lassnig and prints and sculptures by Van Rampelberg, and it was the first presentation of works by both Armitage and Lassnig in East Africa.

According to the exhibition text, the project grew out of conversations between Armitage and KUB's Thomas D. Trummer while they prepared Armitage's 2023 exhibition at the museum. Armitage shaped the selection himself, with attention to influence, lineage and artistic affinity. The three artists share a sustained engagement with the body: Lassnig with what she called "body awareness", Armitage with bodies set in social and political landscapes, and Van Rampelberg with sculptural and print works that distil human presence into contemplative forms.

ART AFRICA, which reviewed the exhibition on 12 February 2026, described the Van Rampelberg works as woodcuts and wooden sculptures, among them male heads with pursed mouths and upright female figures that convey intimacy and relational sensitivity. The exhibition was supported by the Maria Lassnig Foundation, the Federal Ministry of Austria and the Austrian Embassy in Nairobi.

## Why this conversation

Lineage is the exhibition's subject and the talk's setting. The two artists belong to different generations and work in different media, and Armitage has said that he regards Lassnig as one of the most important painters of all time. A conversation between him and Van Rampelberg places a Kenyan sculptor, rather than a European painter, at the centre of that lineage, in the city where she has worked. For visitors who had already seen the gallery's drawings, lithographs and carved figures, the talk offered a chance to hear the two artists in the same room.

NCAI's archive of public programmes includes earlier talks with Van Rampelberg. In September 2021 she joined Wangechi Mutu and Magdalene Odundo DBE for an online panel on sculpture, and NCAI has also published a conversation between her and Fatima Hagi.

The 21 February talk belonged to the exhibition's public programme and required registration, which NCAI's listing now shows as closed.

title: Canon Griffin Rumanzi and Trevor Mukholi in Conversation
standfirst: On 13 September 2025, the artist and the curator of Looking into the Mad Eye of History Without Blinking spoke at NCAI in a talk moderated by Don Handa.
bodyMarkdown:
At the Nairobi Contemporary Art Institute on Saturday 13 September 2025, from 12:00 to 14:00, the artist Canon Griffin Rumanzi and the curator Trevor Mukholi took part in a conversation moderated by Don Handa. NCAI's listing placed the talk in the context of Rumanzi's ongoing solo exhibition, Looking into the Mad Eye of History Without Blinking, and said it would offer "an unflinching glimpse into the exhibition from both curatorial and artistic perspectives." This report draws on that listing and on the exhibition materials. It does not reconstruct what was said.

## The two perspectives

Rumanzi, born in Uganda in 1991, works with digital collage, photography and research. Government seals, colonial papers, family portraits, anonymous snapshots and press images are cut and layered into photomontages. Trevor Mukholi curated the exhibition. Don Handa moderated.

The pairing follows from how the show was made. In ART AFRICA's review of the exhibition, published on 9 September 2025, the critic wrote that Mukholi paced the works to encourage shifts between distance and proximity: from afar, compositions read as unified fields, and up close their layered construction becomes legible. An artist's account of how an image was assembled and a curator's account of how a room was arranged answer different questions, and the talk was set up to hear both.

## What the exhibition asks

The exhibition ran from 11 September to 2 November 2025, so the talk came two days after the opening. Its title describes the guiding idea, a commitment to regard history as it is without hurrying toward a narrative that contains it easily. The exhibition text draws on the writer Ashraf Jamal to say that looking into the "mad eye of history" means rejecting simple stories of heroes and villains, and seeing the whole splintered picture.

The exhibition text says Rumanzi situates Uganda's past within global questions of connectivity, technology and conflict. His method, layering colonial documents, state symbols, family portraits and everyday images, produces what it calls a visual grammar of fracture. Works such as Abaddu Working; We Are All Slaves (2020), which ART AFRICA discussed, compress historical time into a single frame.

## The archive behind the work

Rumanzi's practice extends beyond the gallery. In 2011 he co-founded History in Progress Uganda (HIPUganda) with the artist and educator Andrea Stultiens. It is a public archive that digitises and republishes photographs from or about Uganda's past, and it is dedicated to making the country's visual history accessible and contestable. His collaborations and workshops have involved institutions including the Uganda Press Photo Award/FOTEA, Makerere University Library and Uganda Christian University.

For NCAI, which is itself developing an East African art archive, the exhibition connected two lines of its work: showing contemporary practice, and thinking about how records are kept, described and opened to the public.

## Where it fits

The talk belongs to NCAI's programme of conversations that accompany exhibitions. Here the second voice was the exhibition's curator, which allowed the discussion to address installation and sequence as well as image-making.

The exhibition was Rumanzi's first major solo show in Nairobi, according to ART AFRICA. Registration for the talk is now closed. What remains is the exhibition's documentation, the HIPUganda archive, and the works themselves.
